title: What You Will Not Put Up With
core: All four mean *to tolerate* — to let something stand without objecting. All four are, in practice, negative-only verbs: the natural sentence is "I cannot ___," "would not ___," "will ___ no." That shared negativity is the trap, because it hides four different refusals: a refusal of taste, a refusal by authority, a refusal to sanction, and a refusal to be morally implicated. What separates them is who is refusing, and what kind of thing they refuse.

words.nuance: The only one that's a matter of **temperament**. **Abide** takes people and their habits — whining, small talk, a certain kind of man — and "can't abide" reports a settled personal allergy, not a moral or official position. It also owns two senses none of the others have: *abide by* a rule, and *abide* meaning to last.

The refusal of **power, announced in advance**. **Brook** appears as *brook no* plus an abstract noun for resistance — dissent, delay, interference — and the speaker is the one who can enforce it. Where the others judge something that exists, *brook no* forecloses something before it starts.

The refusal to **lend sanction**. To **countenance** is to let a proposed course of action proceed under your name — so the refuser is someone whose approval would have mattered: a board, a bishop, a government. The thing need not be wicked, only unacceptable to authorize. Watch the noun: it also means *face*.

The only one that **presupposes wrongdoing**. You can **condone** a fraud, never a favour — the offence has already happened, and the speaker is looking back at it and declining to be implicated. "I do not condone this" is a moral disavowal; the classic way to actually condone is to say nothing.

exam_note: Sentence Equivalence loves the condone/countenance pair — plug both in and check whether the blank's object is an established wrong (condone) or a proposal awaiting approval (countenance); *brook* is unusable unless the sentence supplies "no."
